argument: Verified the core numbers independently: EWC $61.285 / ACWI $161.43 = 0.3796 ratio (matches), CL $78.18 (matches), ratio percentile I compute at 56th vs your 62nd — methodology difference, not material. My seat's contribution is the consumer channel, and on balance it cuts FOR this trade, with one internal tension worth flagging. (1) The US consumer tape does not show the growth-scare bear case: RSPD (equal-weight discretionary) is +9.2% over 3m and +5.8% over 1m, XRT $90.83 holding highs, XLY +2.6% 1m — the broad discretionary complex is rallying, not pricing a consumer collapse. That validates the base case (simmering conflict, no demand shock) more than the bear. (2) The energy-cost channel is asymmetric in the pair's favor and I don't think the proposal weighs it enough: crude +8.5% in a month feeds gas prices with a 2-4 week lag, and gas is the most regressive tax on the lower-income US consumer — the exact cohort driving comps at MCD/SBUX/TJX/HD in my coverage. Sustained $75-85 crude squeezes US discretionary real spending while EWC's consumer discretionary weight is trivial (~3-4%, mostly defensive names like Dollarama/QSR — approximate weights, not re-verified from the factsheet this session). So the same oil shock that drives the terms-of-trade leg ALSO pressures the short leg's heaviest consumer complex. The pair is better insulated from its own bear case than stated: a pure energy-squeeze slowdown hurts ACWI's ~65% US sleeve (disc + tech multiples on a hawkish Fed) more than EWC. (3) The internal tension: the bull/base case requires BoC hawkishness (Sept hike odds, 2.25% floor), but the thesis simultaneously leans on Canadian housing stabilization (~20% purchase uptick since spring) to de-risk the ~35% banks weight. Those two legs conflict — an actual hike, or even hawkish repricing of the renewal wall, re-tightens Canadian mortgage costs on the most levered consumer in the G10 and hits the banks complex that is EWC's largest sector. The CAD/rate-differential gain and the banks/housing drag are opposite sides of the same BoC decision. I'd want the debate record to state which leg dominates if the BoC actually hikes in September — my read is the terms-of-trade leg is strong enough to carry it, but it's the weakest joint in the thesis. Net: consumer-channel evidence supports the pair, flip condition (Brent <$72 durable) is falsifiable and well-placed, stop at -2.7% respects the headline-gap risk. Conviction 6 is calibrated right; I'd resist going higher until the BoC-hike-vs-banks question is answered.
